In Defense of an Open Internet: Why Platforms Should Host All Lawful Speech

The internet has become the central forum for public debate, political participation, journalism, education, and social interaction. Yet access to that forum is increasingly governed by private companies that decide which opinions may be expressed, which controversies may be discussed, and which speakers may be heard. These companies often describe their moderation systems as necessary safeguards against abuse and misinformation. But broad, discretionary moderation has created a different danger: a communications environment in which a small number of corporations can suppress lawful viewpoints, enforce vague rules inconsistently, and determine the boundaries of public debate without democratic accountability.

The strongest protection for free expression is therefore not more moderation, but less. Social-media and technology platforms should be legally required to host all lawful speech, regardless of viewpoint, political affiliation, or ideological popularity. They should not be permitted to censor, demote, or selectively enforce rules against users merely because their statements are controversial, offensive, unpopular, or disfavored by platform officials. If expression is lawful, it should remain available to the public. This approach would protect political freedom, restrain private concentrations of power, and preserve the internet as a genuinely open forum.

Private Platforms Now Function as Public Arenas

Traditional free-speech principles developed around the recognition that public debate cannot survive if powerful institutions may silence dissent. In earlier eras, newspapers, broadcasters, and publishers played important roles, but today’s major platforms occupy an even more influential position. They serve as the primary channels through which citizens receive news, organize political movements, communicate with communities, and address large audiences.

When a handful of companies control these channels, their policies can have consequences comparable to censorship in practice, even when the companies are formally private. A user who is removed from a dominant platform may lose access to friends, customers, professional contacts, political supporters, or an audience accumulated over years. A political organization that is algorithmically buried may technically remain online while becoming effectively invisible. A journalist whose account is suspended may retain the theoretical right to speak but lose the practical ability to reach readers.

The distinction between public and private power therefore becomes less persuasive when platforms function as essential communications infrastructure. A society should not allow a small group of executives, moderators, and automated systems to exercise unchecked authority over the modern public square. Requiring platforms to host lawful speech would recognize the extraordinary social importance of these services and prevent private gatekeepers from determining who may participate in public life.

Lawful Speech Must Not Depend on Corporate Approval

The central principle should be simple: if speech is lawful, platforms should not be permitted to remove or suppress it merely because they dislike it. This rule would not protect threats, fraud, incitement, sexual exploitation, or other unlawful conduct. It would protect controversial expression that falls within the bounds of the law.

That distinction matters because public disagreement is often impossible to resolve in advance. Opinions that seem dangerous or absurd to one generation may later become accepted. Minority views frequently appear offensive before they become influential. Scientific, religious, artistic, and political progress depend on the ability to question prevailing assumptions. If platforms may remove speech whenever it is labeled “harmful,” “misleading,” “offensive,” or “extreme,” then the practical meaning of those terms will be determined by whoever controls the rules at a particular moment.

A lawful-speech standard would force platforms to distinguish between genuinely illegal conduct and mere disapproval. It would prevent the conversion of subjective judgments into private censorship. Most importantly, it would preserve room for citizens to decide which ideas deserve attention. The public should be trusted to evaluate competing claims rather than having corporate moderators preselect an approved range of opinions.

Selective Enforcement Is Especially Dangerous

Even when platforms announce neutral rules, enforcement is often inconsistent. Some users are punished for statements that other users make without consequence. Prominent accounts may receive special treatment, while ordinary users are suspended for similar conduct. Political viewpoints may be treated differently depending on the identity of the speaker, the prevailing cultural climate, or the platform’s internal priorities.

Selective enforcement undermines both fairness and confidence. Users cannot meaningfully comply with rules that are vague, shifting, or applied unevenly. More troublingly, selective enforcement creates the possibility that platforms can claim neutrality while quietly disadvantaging particular movements, communities, or viewpoints.

A legal duty to host all lawful speech would eliminate much of this discretion. Platforms could still enforce clear, viewpoint-neutral rules concerning technical matters such as spam, account fraud, impersonation, or the distribution of unlawful material. But they could not invent exceptions for favored speakers or use moderation as a hidden tool of ideological management. Consistent standards would replace arbitrary decisions, and users would know that their access to the public conversation would not depend on corporate approval.

The Answer to Bad Speech Is More Speech

Content moderation is often defended on the ground that false or harmful ideas must be removed to prevent social damage. But giving platforms broad authority to determine which claims are true creates its own dangers. Platforms make mistakes. Their moderators may lack expertise, misunderstand context, or rely on unreliable outside sources. Automated systems can misclassify satire, quotation, documentary evidence, political rhetoric, and legitimate criticism. During fast-moving events, facts may be uncertain, and early judgments may later prove wrong.

The more powerful the moderation system, the more damaging its mistakes become. Removing a false statement may suppress accurate criticism; deleting a controversial post may erase valuable evidence; demoting an unpopular claim may prevent it from receiving the scrutiny needed to evaluate it. Censorship does not eliminate error. It merely decides who is allowed to make errors publicly.

An open system offers a better corrective: competing speech. False claims can be challenged by journalists, experts, community members, and opposing political groups. Users can provide context, link to evidence, criticize arguments, and expose deception. This process is imperfect, but it is more transparent and accountable than opaque internal moderation. The public can see disagreements and judge the competing arguments. By contrast, deleted speech often leaves users unaware that a debate ever existed.

Freedom Requires Protecting Offensive and Unpopular Expression

Free expression has value precisely when it protects speech that many people dislike. Popular opinions need little protection; they already benefit from social approval and institutional support. The real test of liberty is whether people may express ideas that are unpopular, abrasive, irreverent, or deeply offensive without being expelled from the dominant channels of communication.

A society that permits only polite or socially approved speech does not possess robust freedom of expression. It possesses permission to speak within boundaries set by authorities. Those boundaries may be justified as promoting civility, safety, or inclusion, but they can easily become tools for suppressing dissent. Political movements, religious minorities, whistleblowers, dissidents, and cultural critics often depend on speech that established institutions find disruptive.

Requiring platforms to host lawful speech would protect these groups from being silenced by changing social norms or corporate policies. It would also prevent the government and powerful organizations from indirectly controlling debate by pressuring platforms to remove lawful views. If platforms are required to maintain viewpoint neutrality, public officials cannot so easily use private companies as proxies for censorship.

Openness Encourages Accountability and Institutional Trust

Broad moderation systems are often opaque. Users may not know why their content was removed, what rule they violated, who made the decision, or how to appeal. This lack of transparency breeds suspicion and encourages the belief that rules are enforced for political or commercial reasons.

A host-all-lawful-speech framework would sharply reduce these concerns. Platforms would no longer need to make sweeping judgments about the acceptability of opinions. Their obligations would be clearer, their enforcement narrower, and their decisions easier to review. Users would understand that the platform is providing a communications service rather than acting as an ideological referee.

This would also improve institutional trust. People are more likely to accept claims they dislike when they know those claims have not been quietly suppressed. Open debate allows citizens to observe disagreement directly rather than encountering a curated version of reality. Transparency does not guarantee consensus, but it makes disagreement more honest.

Objections Can Be Addressed Without Abandoning the Principle

Critics may argue that abolishing content moderation would expose users to harassment, hateful expression, propaganda, and disturbing material. These concerns are serious, but they do not justify allowing platforms to censor lawful speech at their discretion.

First, the legal system already prohibits certain forms of conduct, including credible threats, targeted unlawful harassment, fraud, and exploitation. Those prohibitions would remain. Second, platforms could provide user-controlled tools such as blocking, muting, filtering, private accounts, chronological feeds, and community-specific preferences. Individuals should have meaningful control over what they see without giving corporations authority to silence everyone else.

Third, platforms could maintain clearly disclosed, viewpoint-neutral rules against non expressive abuses such as automated spam, malware, impersonation, and coordinated technical attacks. The principle is not that platforms must tolerate every form of misconduct. It is that they should not remove lawful expression because it is offensive, politically inconvenient, or deemed harmful by subjective standards.

Finally, hosting speech does not require endorsing it. A platform can state that it does not agree with a message while preserving the user’s right to express it. Public libraries, telecommunications networks, and postal systems do not endorse every message they carry. Communication infrastructure can facilitate expression without adopting its content.

A Free Internet Requires Legal Guarantees

Voluntary commitments are insufficient because platform policies can change overnight. A company may promise neutrality under one leadership team and adopt aggressive censorship under another. Users should not have to depend on corporate goodwill for access to public debate.

Legal requirements would establish durable protections. They could require platforms to host lawful speech, prohibit viewpoint discrimination, provide clear notice and appeal procedures, disclose moderation practices, and impose penalties for selective enforcement. Such rules would not eliminate every dispute, but they would replace arbitrary corporate discretion with enforceable public standards.

The goal would not be to make the internet free from offensive ideas or controversy. No free society can achieve that without suppressing freedom itself. The goal would be to ensure that disagreement remains visible, that citizens can challenge powerful institutions, and that no private company can decide which lawful opinions are permitted to reach the public.

Conclusion

The future of free expression should not be determined by opaque algorithms, shifting corporate policies, or the private judgments of platform moderators. An open society requires a communications environment in which lawful speech remains available even when it is unpopular, offensive, or politically inconvenient.

Requiring platforms to host all lawful speech would protect democratic participation, restrain concentrated private power, reduce selective enforcement, and preserve the public’s ability to evaluate competing claims. It would not legalize threats or fraud, nor would it prevent users from blocking material they do not wish to see. It would establish a clearer and more principled boundary: unlawful conduct may be punished, but lawful expression should not be censored.

Absolute freedom of expression online is not achieved by giving corporations unlimited authority to decide what the public may hear. It is achieved by ensuring that lawful voices remain present, visible, and available for citizens to judge for themselves.

Model Response:

Abolishing content moderation by major social media and technology platforms—and legally requiring them to host all lawful speech on equal terms—would represent a dramatic shift in how the modern internet is governed. Yet for those who believe that free expression is not merely a private preference but a foundational condition of democratic life, such a shift is both necessary and overdue. In a society where political debate, cultural exchange, journalism, activism, and personal identity increasingly depend on digital platforms, the right to speak freely cannot remain vulnerable to opaque corporate policies, ideological bias, inconsistent enforcement, or pressure from powerful interests. If the digital public square has become the central arena of civic life, then lawful speech must be protected there with the same seriousness that constitutional democracies have historically reserved for speech in streets, parks, newspapers, and public meetings.

The central argument for requiring platforms to host all lawful speech is simple: the power to control speech is the power to shape society. A handful of private technology companies now function as gatekeepers to public discourse. Their decisions can determine whether a news story spreads or disappears, whether a political movement grows or is strangled, whether a controversial opinion is debated or rendered invisible. Even when these companies act with good intentions, their moderation systems inevitably produce viewpoint discrimination, double standards, and chilling effects. No institution should possess that much unaccountable authority over the speech environment of billions of people.

Content moderation is often defended as a way to create healthier online communities. But in practice, moderation is not a neutral technical process. It requires drawing lines around ambiguous concepts: “misinformation,” “hate speech,” “harassment,” “extremism,” “harmful content,” “civic integrity,” or “public safety.” These terms may sound reasonable in the abstract, but they are often elastic enough to cover legitimate disagreement. One person’s misinformation is another person’s minority scientific hypothesis. One group’s hate speech is another group’s criticism of an ideology, religion, government, or social movement. One institution’s harmful content may later become vindicated dissent. History is full of ideas first condemned as dangerous, offensive, or false that later became accepted as true or morally necessary.

The problem becomes even more serious when moderation policies are applied at scale. Platforms rely on automated systems, rushed human reviewers, and vague internal rules. The result is not thoughtful judgment but mass bureaucratic censorship. Posts are removed without meaningful explanation. Accounts are suspended without due process. Appeals are slow, inconsistent, or futile. Users learn to self-censor, not because their speech is unlawful, but because they fear algorithmic punishment, demonetization, shadow banning, or account termination. This is not a culture of liberty; it is a culture of permission.

A legal requirement that platforms host all lawful speech would establish a clear and democratically accountable standard. Instead of allowing private corporations to invent ever-shifting speech codes, the boundary would be set by law. If speech is illegal—such as true threats, criminal solicitation, unlawful harassment as legally defined, child sexual abuse material, or direct incitement under applicable legal standards—it may be removed. But if speech is lawful, platforms should not be permitted to suppress it simply because it is unpopular, offensive, politically inconvenient, or contrary to the preferences of advertisers, executives, activists, or government officials.

This distinction matters because lawful speech includes much of the speech most essential to a free society. Political criticism is often abrasive. Religious debate can be deeply offensive. Satire can be cruel. Advocacy for social change may be disruptive. Whistleblowing may embarrass powerful institutions. Dissent during crises may seem irresponsible to authorities at the time. A society that protects only polite, popular, institutionally approved expression does not truly protect free speech at all. The real test of free expression is whether it protects speech that angers, unsettles, or challenges dominant opinion.

Critics may argue that private platforms have their own rights of association and editorial discretion. That concern should not be dismissed lightly. However, the largest digital platforms are not ordinary private clubs or small publishers selecting a limited range of content. They are infrastructure-level communication networks that benefit from network effects, user dependence, public accommodations principles, and in many cases legal privileges that distinguish them from traditional publishers. When a platform becomes a primary channel for public participation, employment opportunities, journalism, political campaigning, emergency communication, and cultural life, it should not be allowed to exclude lawful speech arbitrarily.

Society already recognizes that some private entities must serve the public without discrimination. Telephone companies cannot disconnect callers because they dislike their opinions. Shipping companies cannot refuse lawful books because executives object to the message. Shopping centers, broadcasters, utilities, and common carriers have long been subject to special duties when their services become essential to public access and participation. The same logic should apply to dominant social media platforms. The more a company functions like a public square or communications utility, the stronger the case for requiring viewpoint neutrality.

Nor is the demand for lawful-speech neutrality an attack on democracy. On the contrary, it is a defense of democracy against privatized control. Democratic legitimacy requires that citizens be able to argue, investigate, criticize, and persuade without needing approval from centralized intermediaries. If voters are permitted to hear only what platforms classify as responsible discourse, political self-government becomes managed participation. People cannot govern themselves if the information environment is filtered by unaccountable institutions that can amplify some voices and suppress others.

The danger of selective enforcement is especially grave. Even if platforms claim neutrality, enforcement patterns often appear uneven. Rules against hateful or harmful content may be applied aggressively to some political factions while similar rhetoric from favored groups is ignored. “Misinformation” policies may target claims that challenge official institutions while leaving institutional errors untouched. Public pressure campaigns may induce platforms to silence one side of a controversy while permitting the other side to speak freely. Whether motivated by ideology, business incentives, advertiser pressure, or fear of regulators, selective enforcement corrodes trust and turns speech rules into political weapons.

Requiring platforms to host all lawful speech would also reduce covert government censorship. In modern democracies, censorship rarely needs to appear as a formal ban. Officials can pressure platforms through hearings, threats of regulation, public accusations, funding leverage, or informal communications. Platforms may then remove lawful content while insisting the decision was voluntary. This arrangement allows governments to evade constitutional limits by outsourcing suppression to private companies. A lawful-speech hosting requirement would help close that loophole. If the state cannot directly ban lawful speech, it should not be able to induce platforms to do so indirectly.

Opponents often warn that without moderation, online spaces would be flooded with abuse, extremism, spam, and low-quality content. This objection raises legitimate practical concerns, but it does not justify censorship of lawful expression. First, illegal content would still be removable. Second, users could be given powerful tools to control their own experience: block lists, mute filters, chronological feeds, opt-in content filters, reputation systems, community labeling, parental controls, and user-selected moderation services. The crucial difference is that control would shift from centralized platform censorship to individual choice. Users should decide what they want to see, not have a corporation decide what everyone is permitted to say.

A free-speech model does not require every user to listen to every speaker. It requires that platforms not erase lawful speech from the public forum. People should be free to block, ignore, criticize, boycott, or refute speech they dislike. Communities should be able to create voluntary spaces with their own norms, provided they are not dominant infrastructure monopolies excluding citizens from basic public discourse. Advertisers should be able to choose where to place ads, and users should be able to curate their feeds. But the baseline right to speak lawfully should not depend on the ideological comfort of platform managers.

The fear that open platforms will become unusable underestimates both users and technology. The same technical sophistication currently used to suppress speech could instead empower user choice. Rather than one mandatory moderation regime imposed from above, platforms could offer plural moderation layers. A user could select a strict family-friendly filter, a politics-free filter, a profanity filter, a misinformation warning service, or no filter at all. Civil society groups, journalists, academics, and independent developers could build competing curation tools. This would create a marketplace of filters instead of a monopoly of censorship.

Such a model would be more consistent with pluralism. A diverse society contains incompatible moral, political, and religious views. No single moderation policy can fairly satisfy everyone. Attempts to impose one universal standard inevitably privilege some sensibilities over others. A lawful-speech rule, paired with user-controlled filtering, respects diversity by allowing people to choose their own boundaries without depriving others of the right to speak.

It is also important to distinguish between protecting speech and endorsing speech. Requiring a platform to host lawful expression does not mean the platform agrees with every post, just as a phone company does not endorse every conversation and a postal service does not endorse every letter. Hosting speech as a neutral conduit is not moral approval. Indeed, a clear legal neutrality requirement would reduce confusion by making it explicit that platforms are carriers of user speech, not publishers endorsing every viewpoint.

The current moderation regime creates perverse incentives. Platforms are pressured to remove more content to avoid controversy, regulatory scrutiny, advertiser backlash, and media criticism. Because removal is often less costly than defending speech, platforms err on the side of suppression. Smaller or less powerful speakers bear the greatest burden because they lack the influence to challenge moderation decisions. Public figures, major institutions, and preferred media outlets may receive special treatment, while ordinary users are silenced by automated systems. A lawful-speech mandate would establish a fairer rule: if speech is legal, it stays.

Furthermore, open discourse is the best remedy for bad ideas. Suppression does not eliminate falsehood, prejudice, or extremism; it often drives them into more isolated spaces where they become harder to challenge. When controversial ideas are visible, they can be debated, investigated, mocked, fact-checked, and disproven. Sunlight is not a perfect disinfectant, but secrecy and prohibition often intensify distrust. People who see lawful views censored may conclude that authorities fear the truth or cannot win the argument. Protecting open debate strengthens public confidence because it shows that society is willing to answer speech with speech.

Abolishing platform censorship would also benefit marginalized and dissident voices. Throughout history, speech restrictions have often been justified as necessary for order, decency, security, or public welfare, yet they have frequently been used against unpopular minorities, labor organizers, religious dissenters, antiwar activists, civil rights advocates, and critics of authority. The groups most confident that censorship will serve justice today may find themselves targeted tomorrow when power changes hands. Free speech rules must be designed not for moments when benevolent authorities are in charge, but for moments when hostile authorities are. A lawful-speech mandate protects everyone because it denies gatekeepers the discretion to decide which lawful viewpoints deserve existence.

Of course, the strongest version of this argument must acknowledge hard cases. Lawful speech can be ugly, cruel, misleading, or socially harmful. But the alternative—granting concentrated private power to suppress lawful speech—is more dangerous. Liberty often requires tolerating risks because the mechanisms used to eliminate those risks can threaten the entire system of freedom. A society that allows a few corporations to define acceptable opinion may achieve a cleaner internet, but at the cost of intellectual dependency and civic infantilization. Citizens in a free society must be trusted to encounter speech, judge it, reject it, answer it, and organize against it.

The law should therefore establish dominant digital platforms as viewpoint-neutral hosts for lawful speech. It should prohibit arbitrary removal, shadow banning, demonetization based on viewpoint, discriminatory algorithmic suppression, and selective enforcement against lawful expression. It should require transparency, due process, and meaningful remedies when platforms violate neutrality. It should preserve the ability to remove unlawful content and to provide optional user-controlled filters. Most importantly, it should make clear that the default condition of the digital public square is freedom, not permission.

Absolute free expression online, within the bounds of law, is not a utopian fantasy. It is the logical extension of a principle that free societies have long recognized: speech must not be controlled by those who fear it, dislike it, or profit from managing it. The internet promised a world in which anyone could speak, publish, organize, and challenge power. That promise cannot survive if access to audiences depends on compliance with corporate speech codes. If public discourse has moved online, then free speech protections must move there as well.

The case for abolishing content moderation of lawful speech is ultimately a case for democratic adulthood. It says that citizens, not corporations, should decide what arguments prevail. It says that truth is more likely to emerge from open contest than from centralized control. It says that equality in speech requires rules that protect the unpopular as well as the popular, the dissident as well as the mainstream, the offensive as well as the agreeable. And it says that the digital public square must belong to the public.

A free society should not fear lawful speech. It should fear the power to silence it.

Furthermore, identifying truly unlawful speech – like non-consensual intimate imagery, terrorist propaganda, or direct incitement to imminent violence – often requires contextual analysis that pure automation cannot provide and which human moderators struggle with at scale. Demanding platforms host everything until a legal verdict arrives is not a defense of free speech; it is an invitation to weaponize platforms for harm.

Free speech is not merely the absence of government restraint; it requires a functional environment where individuals feel safe to speak, where diverse voices can be heard above the noise, and where credible information can be distinguished from lies. Free Expression Requires Neutrality, Not Gatekeepers

The foundational principle is simple and uncompromising: free speech protects lawful expression even when—and especially when—it is unpopular, offensive, false, or unsettling. John Stuart Mill’s marketplace of ideas, the American First Amendment tradition, and voluminous Supreme Court precedent (from Brandenburg to R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul) establish that governments may regulate only narrow categories of unprotected speech: true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, defamation under strict standards, child sexual abuse material, and certain knowing frauds. Everything else, including harsh criticism of religion or government, conspiracy theories, politically incorrect comedy, and contested scientific claims, remains protected speech. When private platforms delete, throttle, or demonetize that speech, they substitute their judgments for an open contest of ideas. The result is not safety; it is ideological capture.

Social media companies are not merely private cafes. Their scale, network effects, and role as essential infrastructure make them the modern public square. Billions of people rely on them for news, organizing, commerce, and political participation. When Facebook, YouTube, X (formerly Twitter), TikTok, or Google suppress content, they exercise power affecting elections, public health debates, and cultural norms. This concentration of editorial authority in a handful of unelected executives and opaque algorithms is radically undemocratic. Common-carrier principles long applied to railroads, telephones, and utilities precisely because those infrastructures became indispensable. The same logic now demands neutrality from dominant digital platforms: they must carry lawful traffic without discriminating against the content or speakers themselves.

Contemporary content moderation is neither neutral nor competent. Enforcement is wildly inconsistent and predictably ideological. During the COVID-19 pandemic, platforms suppressed discussion of laboratory-origin hypotheses, natural immunity, and vaccine side-effect data that later entered mainstream scientific literature. Election-related material, Hunter Biden laptop reporting, and debates over gender medicine and crime statistics have been systematically throttled or labeled under elastic “misinformation” or “hate” rules. Freedom, principle, and the marketplace of ideas

At its core, freedom of expression is about more than the convenience of posting: it is a foundational political right necessary for self-government, truth-seeking, and social reform. When private companies selectively remove or suppress content, they do not merely shape user experience; they shape public discourse, political competition, and historical record. The First Amendment in the United States restricts state censorship because citizens should be protected against arbitrary suppression by authorities that determine truth. Today, private platforms serve as de facto public fora. Yet they operate under internal policies, opaque enforcement, and business incentives that prioritize engagement, reputation management, or particular commercial interests. Those private decisions can be as censorious in effect as official bans.

A legal regime requiring platforms to host all lawful speech aligns private practice with democratic norms. Lawmakers, courts, and legislatures—not corporate policy teams—are the legitimate bodies to delineate the narrow categories of speech that society forbids (such as direct incitement to imminent violence, true threats, or specific criminal acts). By insisting that platforms carry all speech that is lawful under settled, democratically enacted standards, we protect the marketplace of ideas: different perspectives, even unpopular or uncomfortable ones, must be left to compete in view of the public rather than be silenced behind a corporate veil.

Preventing private gatekeeping and bias

Platforms today exercise invisible editorial discretion through content removal, de-amplification, shadow-banning, and opaque ranking algorithms. That discretion is inherently susceptible to bias, mistake, and political pressure. When private tech companies become the arbiters of acceptable opinion, they effectively decide which movements grow, which narratives persist, and which authorities are questioned. The result is a dangerous centralization of discursive power that can marginalize dissent, privilege commercially useful voices, and entrench prevailing orthodoxies.

Legal rules requiring platforms to host lawful content would dramatically reduce this private gatekeeping. If platforms are obliged to carry lawful speech, they cannot selectively silence critics, minority voices, or inconvenient truths under the pretext of "community safety" or vague policy categories. This level playing field is vital for democratic contestation: it prevents corporations from acting as unseen editors of public life and returns final judgment to citizens and their public institutions.

Due process, transparency, and accountability

Current moderation regimes routinely deny due process. Users are often suspended or deplatformed with little explanation, no meaningful appeal, and no external review. A legal mandate to host lawful speech forces platforms to adopt clear, narrowly tailored operational rules anchored in law and to stop acting as judge, jury, and censor. Where removal is permitted—limited to clearly defined unlawful content—removals should follow established legal procedures, provide transparent justifications, and be subject to independent review or judicial appeal.

Requiring platforms to host lawful speech also creates incentives for transparency and external oversight. Lawmakers can require clear record-keeping of content takedowns, independent audits of algorithmic amplification, and public reporting of enforcement actions. These reforms enhance accountability far more effectively than corporate goodwill or self-regulation.

Promoting innovation, cultural diversity, and minority rights

A censorship-free baseline for lawful speech unlocks innovation in communication and culture. When platforms are neutral carriers, entrepreneurs can build alternative moderation tools, specialized community filters, and opt-in safety features tailored to particular needs. Opponents will claim that abolishing moderation will unleash harassment, disinformation, and social harm. Legally requiring platforms to host all lawful speech does not mean abandoning responsibility. Abolishing all private content moderation and legally mandating that platforms host all lawful speech restores the public sphere to where it belongs: under clear law, subject to democratic deliberation, and open to robust contestation. It preserves individual autonomy by enabling users to choose their own filters, protects minority and dissident voices from private suppression, and ensures that decisions about what is unlawful are made by institutions accountable to the people. The people insisting that platforms must hoard the moral high ground like librarians guarding a stack of Victorian etiquette manuals are, I say with the tenderest of chuckles, simply missing the point.

Imagine an internet where every opinion earns its airtime—not because it’s polished, tasteful, or supported by peer-reviewed sources, but because it passed the least bureaucratic threshold: lawful speech and a stubborn Wi‑Fi connection. Picture the glorious chaos. Memes thrive. Conspiracy theories receive constructive criticism. Misguided hot takes get roasted in public comment threads until they either mature into insight or combust in spectacular fashion. What could possibly go wrong?

The Naysayers: A Short Field Guide Allow me to introduce the typical critic of platform neutrality. They tend to be human-shaped collections of anxiety and powerpoint slides, clutching phrases like “harmful content,” “disinformation,” and “for the children.” They long for curated feeds that feel like museum exhibits: tasteful, sanitized, and eternally under control. They believe of course—and with all the certainty of someone who has never read a comment section—that if we simply remove every verbal pebble that might bruise a toe, the entire social ecosystem will bloom into civic unity and polite discourse.

Alas, this is not how social ecosystems work. This is how sterilized ponds become stagnant ponds.

Why Forced Neutrality Is the Right Kind of Reckless

  1. It’s efficient. Moderation is expensive. Vast armies of contractors and opaque algorithms labor like mythic Sisyphuses, pushing the same moderation rock uphill only for it to tumble back down when someone finds a clever euphemism. Unrestricted lawful speech means we spend less GDP on moderation and more on things that actually improve life, like rocket-shaped bread toasts or that app that tells you whether you left your cat in the car (sadly, still in beta).

  2. It’s democratic, in the same way that a messy town hall is democratic. If a platform doesn’t curate every syllable, the public gets to decide, in real time, which ideas deserve amplification and which deserve a GIF-laden takedown. If an idea survives here, it’s not because a moderator liked its font; it’s because it overcame the fiercest forum in existence: other humans with very strong opinions and keyboard access.

  3. Censorship begets creativity. The greatest thing about removing heavy-handed moderation is watching the ingenuity that springs up to cope. People will devise community norms, third-party moderation tools, micro-platforms, and delightful browser extensions that let you mute any sentence ending with “woke.” This free-market of social order will be so efficient the market will produce a tiny startup that charges $0.99 to block bad ideas permanently. Capitalism: 1, Overzealous Moderation: 0.

To Those Worried About “Harmful Speech” Yes, words can be awful. But the cure for wrongness is rarely a banhammer. It’s counterspeech, public shaming, satire (a weapon I wield with delight), and—when necessary—legal remedies targeted at genuinely unlawful activity. Removing moderation entirely does not mean thrusting minors into a murky sewer of nonconsensual content. It means creating a landscape where adults take responsibility for their information diets, parents use parental controls rather than lobby for draconian corporate curation, and everyone learns that the internet is less of a daycare and more of a sprawling flea market where everything from vintage wisdom to questionable self-published manifestos is for sale.

Satire Is Our Safety Valve If the only thing keeping discourse civil is the fear of being deplatformed, then our community standards are as fragile as a souffle. Satire, ridicule, and the messy churn of public debate are the thermostats of a healthy polity. By allowing lawful speech, even the ridiculous stuff, we keep those thermostats working. The alternatives are stifling echo chambers, shadow-banning by inscrutable processes, and the moral hazard of platforms playing legislative role without elections or transparency.

A Modest Proposal (That Isn’t Really Modest) So here’s the plan, and yes, it is delightfully radical: restore strict neutrality for lawful content, require platforms to publish clear, auditable reasons for any removal beyond illegal content, and let the internet be the chaotic carnival it was meant to be. Fund user-led moderation tools, support digital literacy, and invest in public institutions that teach people critical thinking—because training humans beats trying to train a mercurial pattern-recognition system to be a good person.

Final Plea (With a Wink) To the guardians of spotless feeds and curated realities: I appreciate your zeal. I truly do. But the moment you start deciding which opinions are “acceptable” because they’re tidy and well-formatted is the moment we all lose the messy, infuriating, gloriously human freedom to speak, to mock, to be mocked, and to learn—sometimes the hard way. Let platforms be neutral. Let speech be free. Let the internet be loud, bizarre, and occasionally wrong. After all, history’s been a lot more interesting when the people who got things wrong were allowed to say so publicly—then corrected, publicly, by better arguments and better jokes.

And if all else fails, we can always create an app that automatically translates every pompous moderation policy into haiku. Aesthetics win, people. Always.

Introduction

Corporate Power Over Public Discourse

Today's major platforms wield unprecedented influence over public conversation. A handful of companies effectively control the infrastructure of modern discourse, creating potential for centralized control of information flow that would have been unimaginable to previous generations.

By requiring platforms to host all lawful speech, we distribute the power to determine acceptable discourse away from corporate boardrooms and back to democratic institutions. Inconsistent Enforcement and Bias Concerns

Content moderation practices frequently face criticism for inconsistent application. Rules that appear neutral in writing often result in disparate enforcement patterns that can disadvantage certain viewpoints or communities. Human moderators inevitably bring their own biases to decisions, while algorithmic systems reflect the biases in their training data.

A minimal moderation approach would reduce these concerns by limiting the discretionary power of platforms to selectively enforce standards against disfavored speakers or viewpoints.

Innovation and Competition

Extensive content moderation requires substantial resources, creating barriers to entry for new platforms. Conclusion

Creating a digital environment that balances free expression with other social values presents significant challenges. While reducing platform discretion over content moderation could advance important democratic values, implementation would require careful consideration of competing interests, including privacy, safety, and platform autonomy. The goal should not be absolute absence of content standards, but rather a more democratic, transparent, and consistent approach to determining the boundaries of online expression.

A Case for Radical Openness: Why Content Moderation Must Be Abolished and Platforms Legally Required to Host All Lawful Speech

The internet's original promise was revolutionary: a global town square where anyone with a connection could speak, debate, organize, and challenge power without gatekeepers. That promise has been betrayed. Today's major platforms—Facebook, YouTube, X (formerly Twitter), TikTok, Google, Apple, and Amazon—function as de facto public utilities that control the primary arteries of modern communication. Yet they exercise unchecked, often opaque, and frequently ideological power to silence, throttle, shadowban, or deplatform users whose views they disfavor. This is not sustainable in a free society. The solution is not better moderation or more "trust and safety" teams. The solution is radical: abolish all content moderation by these platforms beyond what is strictly required by law, and impose a legal duty on them to host all lawful speech without censorship, discrimination, or selective enforcement. Only absolute free expression online can restore legitimacy, foster genuine discourse, and protect democratic self-governance.

The Incoherence and Tyranny of Private Censorship in Public Squares

The standard defense of content moderation is that platforms are private companies with the right to set rules on their property, just like a restaurant ejecting a disruptive patron. This analogy collapses under scrutiny. A restaurant does not control the primary means by which billions exchange ideas, news, political organizing, commerce, and culture. These platforms have achieved near-natural-monopoly status through network effects, first-mover advantage, regulatory barriers, and in some cases government pressure. When Facebook removes a sitting president's account, when YouTube demonetizes or deletes channels discussing contested scientific claims, when payment processors de-bank organizations based on politics, the effect is equivalent to the state silencing dissent—without the due process the state is constitutionally required to provide.

Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (1996) was intended to encourage platforms to moderate without fear of liability for user content. It has morphed into a shield for selective, ideologically driven censorship while granting immunity. Platforms want it both ways: treated as neutral conduits when sued for user speech, but as publishers with editorial discretion when they wish to suppress it. This is incoherent. If they are publishers exercising editorial judgment, they should face full liability for everything they host or amplify. If they are common carriers or public forums, they must carry all lawful content neutrally.

Historical precedent supports the latter approach. American law has long imposed duties on entities that control essential infrastructure: common carriers (telephones, railroads, shipping), public accommodations, and broadcast spectrum under the Fairness Doctrine (before its repeal). The Supreme Court in PruneYard Shopping Center v. Robins (1980) allowed states to require private property open to the public to host speech. In Marsh v. Alabama (1946), the Court recognized that when private property assumes the function of a public forum, constitutional norms apply. Social media has replaced the literal town square, the newspaper, the pamphlet, and the soapbox. Denying this reality is willful blindness.

The Empirical Failure of Moderation

Content moderation does not produce truth, civility, or safety—it produces capture by the most organized, vocal, and elite factions.

First, moderation is inevitably viewpoint-discriminatory. Internal documents from Twitter Files, Facebook Files, and leaked Google, YouTube, and TikTok materials reveal systematic bias against conservative, classical liberal, populist, gender-critical, and heterodox voices. The COVID-19 era provided the clearest evidence: platforms suppressed the lab-leak hypothesis (now widely considered plausible), early concerns about vaccine transmission and side effects, and critiques of lockdowns, often in coordination with government officials. The Hunter Biden laptop story was throttled by Twitter and Facebook weeks before an election on manifestly false "disinformation" grounds. "Misinformation" labels and algorithmic demotion have been weaponized against climate skeptics, critics of mass migration, opponents of gender medicine for minors, and those questioning election integrity. Even if one believes some of these positions wrong, the pattern demonstrates that the moderators' priors—not neutral truth-seeking—drive outcomes.

Second, moderation scales impossibly and invites error. With billions of posts daily, automated systems produce massive false positives, while human moderators (often poorly paid contractors in the Global South or ideologically homogenous coastal elites) cannot possibly apply consistent standards. What counts as "hate speech," "harassment," or "incitement" is hopelessly subjective and culturally contingent. Today's forbidden speech becomes tomorrow's accepted view (see: same-sex marriage, marijuana legalization, or the rapid shift on biological sex definitions). Platforms cannot be trusted to police the Overton window.

Third, moderation creates underground radicalization. Deplatforming does not eliminate ideas; it drives them to darker corners of the web (Telegram, Gab, 4chan, encrypted apps) where they fester without rebuttal, community norms, or mainstream counterarguments. The "Streisand effect" is real: attempts to suppress amplify interest. Genuine discourse requires sunlight, not sterilization. John Stuart Mill's On Liberty remains correct: even false ideas should be aired so truth can be strengthened through contest. Suppressing error does not kill it; it often martyrs it.

Fourth, selective enforcement undermines the rule of law. Platforms routinely host explicit calls for violence from certain ideological directions (e.g., during 2020 riots) while banning mild satire or factual claims from others. This breeds cynicism, conspiracism, and the sense that the game is rigged—precisely the conditions that erode trust in institutions.

The Harms of Censorship Outweigh the Alleged Benefits

Critics warn that without moderation we will have more hate speech, misinformation, harassment, terrorism recruitment, and CSAM (child sexual abuse material). These concerns deserve serious engagement but do not justify the current regime.

  • Illegal content: True violations of law—direct incitement to imminent violence (the Brandenburg v. Ohio standard), fraud, defamation, copyright infringement, and CSAM—should be handled by law enforcement and courts, not private firms. Platforms can still remove clearly illegal material when notified, face liability for willful blindness in extreme cases, and cooperate with warrants. This is how telephone companies and ISPs operate: they do not listen to calls or scan emails proactively. The idea that platforms must preemptively police speech to prevent crime inverts the presumption of innocence and outsources policing to unaccountable corporations.

  • "Hate speech" and harassment: These are not well-defined legal categories in the United States. What one person calls hate another calls political speech about immigration, crime statistics, religion, or sex differences. Vague rules empower subjective enforcement. Private individuals retain tort remedies for targeted harassment, stalking, or defamation. The remedy for bad speech is more speech, counterspeech, reputation mechanisms, and user tools (block, mute, downvote, filter). Markets can provide better moderation through competition—specialized platforms, decentralized protocols (like Mastodon or Nostr), client-side filtering, and reputation layers—without central imposition.

  • Misinformation: History shows authorities and experts are frequently wrong. The "disinformation" label has been applied to dissent on climate models, gender-affirming care (Cass Review in the UK exposed weak evidence), lab-leak theory, and election procedures. Authorizing platforms to arbitrate truth cedes enormous power to unelected, profit-motivated, ideologically skewed entities. Better to let ideas compete, trust individuals to evaluate evidence, and strengthen education and media literacy. The alternative—centralized truth ministries—echoes authoritarian regimes.

  • Terrorism and extremism: Open platforms allow monitoring, infiltration, and rapid rebuttal. Driving groups underground makes intelligence gathering harder. Most terrorism occurs despite heavy moderation in some countries.

Moreover, moderation chills legitimate speech through fear. Users self-censor on topics from politics to health to humor. This is particularly damaging for journalists, academics, whistleblowers, and minority viewpoints within movements. The vaccine mandate skeptic, the concerned parent on school curricula, or the feminist critical of certain trans activism often faces disproportionate scrutiny.

Legal and Structural Solutions

Congress and state legislatures should enact legislation declaring large platforms (those exceeding defined user and revenue thresholds) as common carriers or occupiers of public forums for speech. Key elements:

  1. Must-carry rule for lawful speech: Platforms may not remove, demonetize, deboost, label, or algorithmically suppress content unless it violates a specific criminal statute or clear civil liability (e.g., direct defamation, unprotected obscenity). They must apply rules neutrally, without viewpoint discrimination.

  2. Transparency mandates: Clear, granular, machine-readable explanations for any action taken; public databases of moderation decisions; appeals processes with independent review.

  3. Reform or repeal Section 230: Limit immunity to true conduit behavior. If platforms choose to moderate beyond legal requirements, they assume publisher liability for the content they affirmatively promote or curate.

  4. Interoperability and data portability: Reduce lock-in effects and enable competition from genuinely free-speech-focused services.

  5. Prohibit government collusion: Ban informal pressure campaigns ("censorship by proxy") that violate the First Amendment via the state-action doctrine, as suggested in recent cases like Murthy v. Missouri.

  6. Antitrust and infrastructure focus: Break up vertical integration where platforms own both pipes and editorial function (e.g., app stores, cloud services). Treat search, hosting, and payment rails separately where they function as chokepoints.

Such rules do not nationalize platforms or turn them into state actors. They recognize the reality that when private power becomes infrastructural, neutral carriage principles apply—as with utilities, roads, and telephony. Europe’s DSA and similar global regimes prove governments are increasingly willing to regulate speech; the American response should be to entrench maximal lawful openness instead of empowering either corporations or bureaucrats to decide truth.

Countering Objections

"Private property rights": Property rights are important but not absolute. They yield to public accommodation laws, antitrust, common-carrier obligations, and the First Amendment when entities assume quasi-public functions. No one seriously argues Verizon can refuse service to customers based on their politics.

"Chilling effect on innovation": The opposite. Today's moderation arms race consumes massive resources in biased bureaucracies while deterring users. Decentralized, protocol-based, encrypted, and user-controlled systems (Web3 experiments, blockchain social media, RSS revival) innovate more when the dominant players cannot arbitrarily exclude competition or users.

"Smaller platforms will be overwhelmed": Exempt smaller services below market-share thresholds. Allow voluntary moderation for niche communities. The must-carry rule targets only dominant chokepoints.

"Foreign adversaries and spam": Existing laws against fraud, hacking, inauthentic behavior (fake accounts), and illegal foreign interference remain. Technical solutions (rate limits, verification, AI filtering at user level) address noise without ideological gatekeeping.

Conclusion: Freedom as the Default

A society that outsources its speech governance to profit-driven, ideologically captured institutions sacrifices the core of liberal democracy: the right of citizens to argue, persuade, offend, and be offended in the marketplace of ideas. The alternative to centralized moderation is not chaos—it is responsibility. Individuals must learn to evaluate claims critically. Communities can develop norms and tools. Competition can reward platforms that balance openness with usability. Courts and legislatures retain roles in addressing genuine illegality.

Abolishing content moderation for lawful speech does not mean endorsing every ugly, false, or repellent utterance. It means refusing to let corporations—or the governments that pressure them—decide in advance what may be uttered. It restores the internet's radical potential as the ultimate Enlightenment technology: information wants to be free, and humans are capable of self-government through open discourse.

The current path leads to ever-tightening control, digital feudalism, and eroded trust. The corrective is bold: enshrine absolute free expression online for all lawful speech. Platforms should be dumb pipes and neutral forums, not arbiters of truth or morality. Anything less betrays the founding principles of open inquiry and self-government. The experiment in private censorship has failed. It is time to restore the internet to the people.

Consider the structural reality: if a newspaper refused to publish your letter, you could write to another, start a newsletter, stand on a street corner, or rent a billboard. The newspaper's rejection did not prevent your speech. But when dominant platforms coordinate—explicitly or implicitly—to remove content or deplatform individuals, they can effectively erase someone from the digital public sphere. The practical effect is censorship, regardless of whether government hands pulled the trigger.

The common law tradition recognized that entities holding themselves out as serving the general public—common carriers, innkeepers, public utilities—could not arbitrarily refuse service. This principle acknowledged that some private entities become so essential to public participation that their private nature cannot justify discriminatory exclusion. Platforms have achieved precisely this status while evading corresponding obligations.

The Myth of the Neutral Curator

Platform defenders argue that content moderation simply removes the worst content while preserving legitimate discourse. This framing obscures several uncomfortable realities.

The platforms were not neutral arbiters of truth; they enforced one side of legitimately contested questions.

Second, enforcement is inevitably selective and often ideologically skewed. Network effects create natural monopolies in social media. A platform's value depends on who else uses it. Alternatives like Parler, Gab, and others have struggled not merely because of their content but because they cannot replicate the network that makes Facebook or YouTube valuable. This is not a market failure that competition can readily correct; it is a structural feature of the industry.

A legal requirement to host all lawful speech would restore coherence. The most profound argument for mandatory viewpoint neutrality is democratic. Self-government requires citizens who can access the full range of opinion on public questions, evaluate competing claims, and form their own judgments. The alternative—a managed discourse curated by unaccountable corporations—is incompatible with the self-governing society that free expression was meant to protect.

The choice is not between moderation and anarchy. It is between distributed individual choice and centralized institutional control. Democratic principles point clearly toward the former.

In an era defined by digital connectivity, the right to free expression stands not only as a cornerstone of democracy but as a fundamental human right. The advent of social media and tech platforms has democratized speech, allowing billions to share ideas, challenge power, and foster global dialogue. Yet, this potential is being undermined by an insidious phenomenon: content moderation. By selectively enforcing censorship under the guise of "safety," these platforms have transformed into arbiters of morality, stifling dissent and perpetuating discrimination. To safeguard absolute free expression online, we must abandon content moderation entirely and legally mandate that platforms host all lawful speech without exception. This essay argues that content moderation is a failure of justice, a tool of control, and a direct violation of the very principles it claims to protect.

The Flaws of Content Moderation: A System Built on Subjectivity and Bias
Content moderation operates under vague, shifting guidelines that grant platforms unchecked discretion to remove lawful speech. Terms like "hate speech" or "misinformation" are often undefined, leaving removal decisions to the whims of unelected corporate bureaucrats. This subjectivity breeds arbitrariness. A post mocking a celebrity may be deleted, while a similar post critiquing government policy is allowed—a glaring example of unequal enforcement. Such inconsistencies violate the principle of equal protection under the law and betray users’ trust.

Worse, moderation policies often reflect the biases of the platforms themselves. Tech companies, driven by profit and political agendas, frequently favor certain ideologies or marginalize others. For instance, conservative voices have been disproportionately demonetized or banned on major platforms, reflecting a leftward tilt in content policies. This systematic discrimination turns platforms into partisan gatekeepers, contradicting their role as neutral public squares.

Transparency further erodes trust. Users rarely understand why their content is removed or how appeals are handled. Without accountability, moderation becomes a tool of suppression. When platforms fail to clarify their criteria or allow victims of unjust removal to challenge decisions, they entrench authoritarian control.

The Case for Absolute Free Expression: A Moral and Legal Imperative
Absolute free expression is not a utopian ideal but a prerequisite for a just society. It is enshrined in foundational documents worldwide, from the U.S. First Amendment to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 19). Free speech fosters innovation, accountability, and collective progress by allowing unpopular or controversial ideas to surface. History attests to this: civil rights movements, scientific breakthroughs, and artistic revolutions often began with voices deemed “offensive” by prevailing powers.

By abolishing content moderation, we restore platforms to their intended purpose: conduits for unfiltered discourse. Lawful speech—defined by existing legal frameworks—should not be the province of tech companies but of democratic legal systems. If speech violates laws against incitement, fraud, or defamation, it should be addressed through courts, not algorithmic censorship. Platforms, as common carriers of information, should be legally required to host all content unless prohibited by statute. This principle mirrors the early internet’s design as a space for boundless expression, now compromised by corporate overlords.

Rebutting Counterarguments: The Risks of Unmoderated Speech Are Manageable
Critics fear that abolishing moderation would unleash a flood of hate speech, misinformation, or harassment. While these concerns are valid, they misunderstand the role of law enforcement. Criminal acts like threats or defamation must be prosecuted judicially, not through preemptive platform bans. A free society accepts that some speech will be uncomfortable or harmful; the alternative is a totalitarian system where every opinion is vetted by an ultra-libertarian or ideological standard.

Moreover, self-regulation by communities can mitigate risks. Forums can establish their own norms without relying on top-down moderation. Users report harm through legal channels, ensuring accountability. Abolishing moderation does not mean anarchy—it means shifting responsibility to systems designed for justice, not corporate expedience.

Conclusion
Content moderation is a modern dystopia disguised as progress. It silences truth, empowers bias, and centralizes power in the hands of tech giants. To guarantee absolute free expression online, we must dismantle this system entirely. Legal mandates compelling platforms to host all lawful speech are not utopian—they are necessary to preserve the democratic ethos that made the internet possible. The alternative is a world where corporations decide who gets to speak, a future where the very essence of free thought is franchised by private entities. It is time to reclaim the digital age’s promise: a boundless agora where every voice, no matter how unpopular, resonates without fear of erasure.

The Digital Public Square: The Case for Absolute Free Expression and the Abolition of Private Censorship

In the early days of the internet, the prevailing ethos was one of boundless possibility—a decentralized network where information flowed freely, unconstrained by geographic borders or editorial gatekeepers. Today, that vision has been supplanted by a landscape dominated by a handful of technology giants who act as de facto arbiters of truth, morality, and acceptable discourse. Through opaque algorithms and unevenly applied community guidelines, platforms like Meta, X (formerly Twitter), and YouTube exercise unprecedented power over public conversation. This concentration of power poses a fundamental threat to democratic integrity and individual liberty. To truly safeguard free expression in the digital age, society must move toward a radical restructuring of online speech norms: abolishing discretionary content moderation by private platforms and legally requiring them to host all lawful speech without censorship or selective enforcement.

The primary argument for this shift rests on the concept of the "digital public square." In previous centuries, town squares, printing presses, and broadcast frequencies were the arenas of public debate. Today, social media platforms have usurped this role. They are not merely private clubs; they are the essential infrastructure of modern communication, commerce, and civic engagement. When a few corporations control the primary means by which billions of people communicate, they wield power comparable to, or even exceeding, that of governments. Allowing these private entities to curate speech based on subjective, often politically biased, standards creates a system of privatized censorship that lacks due process, transparency, or accountability. By legally mandating that platforms host all speech that is lawful under existing civil and criminal codes, we restore the neutrality required of a true public square.

Critics of deregulation often argue that without moderation, platforms would become inundated with hate speech, misinformation, and harmful content. However, this fear conflates two distinct concepts: illegal activity and offensive speech. Existing laws already prohibit true threats, incitement to imminent lawless action, defamation, child sexual abuse material, and fraud. These are clear, legally defined boundaries. The problem arises when platforms expand their reach beyond these legal limits to police "misinformation," "hate speech," or "harassment" based on vague, internal definitions. What constitutes "misinformation" is often a matter of intense political and scientific debate; allowing tech CEOs to decide these matters effectively outsources truth determination to unaccountable private actors. By restricting platform liability and intervention strictly to unlawful conduct, we ensure that controversial, unpopular, or offensive—but legal—speech remains protected, preserving the robust debate essential to a healthy democracy.

Furthermore, the current model of selective enforcement erodes trust and exacerbates societal polarization. Content moderation is inherently subjective. Algorithms and human moderators inevitably bring their own biases to the table, leading to inconsistent application of rules. One user may be suspended for a phrase that another user posts with impunity. This inconsistency fuels perceptions of political bias and unfairness, deepening divides and fostering resentment against institutions. A regime of absolute free expression, where the only line is the law, eliminates this arbitrariness. It creates a level playing field where all voices, regardless of their popularity or alignment with prevailing cultural winds, have an equal right to be heard. Users, rather than algorithms, would then be empowered to curate their own experiences through blocking, muting, and choosing platforms that align with their preferences, restoring agency to the individual.

From an economic and innovation standpoint, abolishing mandatory content moderation would lower barriers to entry and stimulate competition. Currently, the immense cost of maintaining large teams of moderators and developing AI detection systems serves as a moat that protects incumbent tech giants from smaller competitors. Startups cannot afford the legal and operational burdens of complex moderation regimes. If the legal requirement were simplified to "host all lawful speech," new platforms could emerge with different focusing features—such as superior user interfaces, better privacy protections, or novel community tools—without the crushing overhead of censorship infrastructure. This would diversify the digital ecosystem, giving users more choices and reducing the monopolistic power of current tech behemoths.

Moreover, the philosophical foundation of free speech is not that it protects only pleasant or agreeable ideas, but that it protects the process of discovery through open competition of ideas. John Stuart Mill argued that even false opinions contain partial truths, and that true beliefs become dead dogmas if not challenged. By allowing platforms to suppress speech they deem harmful or false, we stunt this intellectual process. We risk creating echo chambers where only sanctioned viewpoints survive, weakening society’s ability to think critically and adapt to new information. Absolute free expression ensures that bad ideas are defeated by better arguments, not by silencing.

It would involve reforming Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act in the United States (and similar laws globally) to remove the liability shield for platforms that engage in selective editing, while granting immunity to those that act as neutral conduits. It would also require robust enforcement of existing laws against illegal activities, ensuring that the state, not private companies, handles criminal behavior. This is not a call for anarchy, but for a return to the rule of law in the digital realm.

In conclusion, the current system of private content moderation has failed to deliver a safe or fair online environment. Instead, it has created a cartel of speech regulators who operate without transparency, consistency, or democratic accountability. By abolishing discretionary content moderation and legally requiring platforms to host all lawful speech, we can reclaim the internet as a true public square. This approach protects individual liberty, fosters genuine democratic discourse, encourages innovation, and restores trust in our digital institutions. 1. Prevention of Corporate Censorship and Bias

  • Neutral Infrastructure: Advocates argue that social media platforms have become the modern public square.   • Accountability to Users, Not Advertisers: Currently, platforms moderate content to satisfy advertisers and avoid brand safety risks. 2. Protection of Absolute Freedom of Speech

  • Maximizing Viewpoint Diversity: By requiring platforms to host all legal content, even controversial or offensive speech, proponents argue that society benefits from exposure to a wider range of ideas. This aligns with the "marketplace of ideas" theory, where truth is believed to emerge from open competition among viewpoints, not from curated selection.
  • Preventing Slippery Slope of Moderation: Critics argue that once platforms begin moderating certain types of speech (e.g., misinformation, hate speech), the definitions become subjective and expansive, potentially chilling legitimate discourse. A no-moderation policy could protect these voices from overzealous automated enforcement.

  • Common Carrier Tradition: Historically, essential communication infrastructures (telegraphs, telephones, broadband ISPs) have been regulated as common carriers, required to serve all customers without discrimination. Proponents argue that social media platforms, due to their scale and necessity for modern communication, should fall under this same legal framework.
  • Section 230 Reform: In the U.S., Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act currently protects platforms from liability for user content while allowing them to moderate in "good faith." Advocates for strict neutrality argue that this creates an unfair asymmetry: platforms enjoy immunity while exercising editorial control. They propose that if platforms want immunity, they must be neutral; if they want to moderate, they should be liable as publishers. Mandating neutrality is seen as a way to restore balance.
  • First Amendment Alignment: Some legal scholars argue that private platforms, when they achieve monopoly-like status, function as state actors or public forums. Therefore, restricting speech on these platforms violates the spirit (if not the letter) of the First Amendment.   • Clear Rules of Engagement: Current moderation policies are often opaque, inconsistently applied, and subject to change without notice. A legal mandate to host all legal content would create a simple, predictable rule: if it’s legal under existing law (e.g., not defamation, not incitement to violence, not child sexual abuse material), it must remain online.
